section_summary: This section contains a fragment of an earlier report, three short State Department memoranda, and the opening 64 pages of a study titled “A Review of Communism in Japan.” The study traces the Japan Communist Party’s history and postwar electoral gains, then examines its reported activities in labor, youth groups, farming, women’s organizations, the press, theater, and education. Its assessments and allegations are those of the contemporary authors.

subfiles.title: Continuation of confidential report on Communist activities
subfiles.about: A report discusses alleged clandestine Communist operatives and Ritsu Ito's denial.
subfiles.summary: Describes alleged unregistered Communist operatives and quotes Ritsu Ito rejecting the claims.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Communist subversive activities in Japan
subfiles.about: An informant urges closer American attention to Communist organizing among police, rural communities, and students.
subfiles.summary: Relays allegations of Communist organizing and recommends investigation of occupation personnel and relief from the purge for Japanese businessmen.

subfiles.title: JCP Appeal to Nationalism
subfiles.about: The memorandum identifies two Japan Communist Party positions framed as appeals to Japanese nationalism.
subfiles.summary: Cites Tokuda's defense statement and party proposals concerning sovereignty, troop withdrawal, and self-defense.

subfiles.to: Mr. Butterworth; Mr. Allison; Mr. Davies; Mr. Hooker
subfiles.about: Bishop circulates an initial Northeast Asian Affairs study of communism in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Introduces the attached study and invites suggestions for continued research.

subfiles.title: A Review of Communism in Japan
subfiles.from: Hillis Lory, Division of Northeast Asian Affairs
subfiles.about: A study reviews the Japan Communist Party's development and alleged influence across Japanese political and social institutions.
subfiles.summary: The study begins with a contents page and summary, then traces the party from its 1920s origins through its postwar reorganization and 1949 electoral gains. It examines party schools and reported activity in labor unions, youth groups, farming, women's organizations, newspapers, theater, and education. Its conclusion argues that economic conditions, political culture, and Communist advances in China could affect the party's future in Japan. The study continues beyond this section.
